'''Sarah Wyatt''' is an American, plant molecular biologist. She is a professor in the Department of Environmental and Plant Biology at [[Ohio University]],<ref name="Ohio">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ohio.edu/cas/plantbio/contact/profiles.cfm?profile=wyatts|title=Sarah Wyatt faculty page, Ohio University|website=www.ohio.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-07-17}}</ref> as well as director of the Ohio University [https://www.ohio.edu/mcb/ Interdisciplinary Graduate Program in Molecular and Cellular Biology]. Wyatt's research interests include [[molecular biology]], [[genomics]], and signaling events.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=yXhk2d4AAAAJ&hl=en|title=Sarah Wyatt|access-date=July 18, 2017}}</ref> She is considered one of the world's experts on gravitational signaling in plants, and some of her recent research includes an experiment on board the [[International Space Station|International Space Station (ISS)]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/heo/slpsra/20130529_spacebio_nraawards.html|title=NASA Selects Space Biology Research Proposals|last=Administrator|first=NASA|date=2016-02-04|work=NASA|access-date=2017-07-18|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/experiments/1181.html|title=NASA - Biological Research in Canisters-20|website=www.nasa.gov|access-date=2017-07-18}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Sarah Wyatt was born in 1958 and raised in [[Mayfield, Kentucky]]. She received her B.S. in Cognition and Development in 1980 and a B.S. in biology in 1984 from the [[University of Kentucky]]. In 1991, she received her M.S. in Plant Pathology, also from the University of Kentucky. She went on to attend [[Purdue University]] and in 1995 received her Ph.D. from the Interdisciplinary Plant Physiology Program.<ref name="Ohio"/>

From 1982 to 1988, Wyatt held a position as a Senior Scientist in Research and Development for Fungal and Parasitic Diseases American Scientific Products in [[Lexington, Kentucky]], after which she was a research assistant in the Department of Plant Pathology at [[Kentucky University]] from 1988 to 1990. In 1994, Wyatt was a visiting scientist at both the [[University of Zurich]] in Zurich, Switzerland, and the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] in Kazan, Russia.<ref name="Ohio"/>

In 2012, while holding a position as Associate Chair in the Department of Environmental and Plant Biology at Ohio University, Wyatt served as "Rotating" Program Director of Integrative and Organismal Systems for the [[National Science Foundation]]. She continued her service to the National Science Foundation as an Intermittent Program Director for Molecular and Cell Biology from 2014 to 2015. Currently, Wyatt is a professor in the Department of Environmental and Plant Biology and Director of the Interdisciplinary Molecular and Cell Biology Program at Ohio University, Athens, Ohio. Her research lab is staffed by both graduate and undergraduate students, who use molecular, genetic and genomic tools to study plant growth and development, with a focus on plant gravitropic signaling.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://wyattlab.wordpress.com|title=Wyatt Lab Wordpress|website=Gravitron|language=en-US|access-date=2017-07-17}}</ref> Other projects in the Wyatt lab involve the shift between [[Chasmogamy|chasmogamous]] (open) and [[Cleistogamy|cleistogamous]] (closed) flowers in ''[[Viola pubescens]]''<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Y.|last2=Ballard|first2=H.E.|last3=Stockinger|first3=E.J.|last4=Nadella|first4=V.|last5=Sternberger|first5=A.L.|last6=Wyatt|first6=S.E.|title=The potential role of two LEAFY orthologs in the chasmogamous/cleistogamous mixed breeding system of Viola pubescens (Violaceae)|journal=The Journal of the Torrey Botanical Society|volume=144|issue=2|pages=206–217|doi=10.3159/TORREY-D-16-00023R2|year=2017|s2cid=90467000}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Y.|last2=Ballard|first2=H.E.|last3=McNally|first3=R.|last4=Wyatt|first4=S.E.|title=Gibberellins are involved but not sufficient to trigger a shift between chasmogamous-cleistogamous flower types in Viola pubescens|journal=The Journal of the Torrey Botanical Society|volume=141|issue=1|pages=1–8|doi=10.3159/TORREY-D-12-00044.1|year=2013|s2cid=83732211}}</ref> and genetic fingerprints indicating gene expression and relationships during evolution of plant species.

== NASA experience and ISS experiment ==
Following her Ph.D., Wyatt became a Research Associate for the NASA Specialized Center of Research and Training in the Department of Botany at [[North Carolina State University]]. She held that position from 1996 to 2000, after which she began her teaching career at Ohio University in the Department of Environmental and Plant Biology.<ref name="Ohio"/> In early 2013, Wyatt submitted a research proposal to NASA's Research Opportunities in Space Biology (ROSBio), and in May of the same year her proposal along with eight others, was accepted for experimentation aboard the [[International Space Station|ISS]].<ref name=":0" /> The objective of her space flight mission, entitled The Biological Research in Canisters<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/experiments/708.html|title=NASA - Biological Research in Canisters|website=www.nasa.gov|access-date=2017-07-18}}</ref>-20 (BRIC-20), was to germinate ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]'' seedlings in space and study their [[Transcriptomics technologies|transcriptomic]] and [[Proteomics|proteomic]] responses to [[Micro-g environment|microgravity]].<ref name=":1" /> In January 2015, the SpaceX Falcon 9<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.spacex.com/falcon9|title=Falcon 9|last=spacexcmsadmin|date=2012-11-15|work=SpaceX|access-date=2017-07-18|language=en}}</ref> was sent into orbit, placing a Dragon cargo capsule with the BRIC-20 experiment<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.spacex.com/dragon|title=Dragon|last=spacexcmsadmin|date=2012-11-15|work=SpaceX|access-date=2017-07-18|language=en}}</ref> in path to the [[Harmony (ISS module)|ISS Harmony module]].<ref name=":2" /> The SpaceX Dragon cargo was released from the ISS after a month of spaceflight and returned to Earth for de-integration at the [[Kennedy Space Center]]. Once de-integrated, samples were shipped to the Wyatt lab at Ohio University for proteomic and transcriptomic analyses. Results of the space flight mission are in press<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kruse|first1=C.P.S.|last2=Basu|first2=P.|last3=Luesse|first3=D.R.|last4=Wyatt|first4=S.E.|title=Transcriptome and proteome responses in RNAlater preserved tissue of Arabidopsis thaliana|journal=PLOS ONE|volume=12|issue=4|article-number=e0175943|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0175943|pmc=5397022|pmid=28423006|year=2017|bibcode=2017PLoSO..1275943K|doi-access=free}}</ref> and under review (see selected publications) and may provide invaluable insight into how plants cope in a microgravity environment, subsequently enhancing efforts to use plants for sources of food and oxygen during future spaceflight missions.<ref name=":1" /> Following the BRIC-20 mission, Wyatt received Faculty Fellowship Leave to work with GeneLab<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://genelab.nasa.gov|title=NASA GeneLab|website=genelab.nasa.gov|language=en|access-date=2017-07-18}}</ref> - Omics Open Science Initiative at the [[Ames Research Center|NASA Ames Research Center]] in [[Mountain View, California]].

== Service and outreach ==
Through her academic career, Wyatt has presented numerous talks, demonstrations, and workshops reaching approximately 2,100 sixth-twelfth grade students, 1,000 elementary aged students, and 80 adults. Wyatt has been the Organizing Committee Chair and a presenter for [[American Association of University Women|AAUW]]'s Tech Savvy program in Athens, Ohio since 2014.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aauw.org/2014/05/28/research-in-space/|title=To Tech Savvy and Beyond: AAUW Member Sends Her Research into Space|website=AAUW: Empowering Women Since 1881|access-date=2017-07-18}}</ref> Tech Savvy is a daylong [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] career conference for middle school girls, aimed at introducing and attracting them to the STEM fields through hands-on activities.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.aauw.org/what-we-do/stem-education/tech-savvy/|title=Tech Savvy|work=AAUW: Empowering Women Since 1881|access-date=2017-07-18|language=en-US}}</ref> Wyatt has been a voluntary member of the Plant Science Definition Team through [[NASA]] since August 2016, and has sat on numerous grant panels including those through [[NASA]], the [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF), the [[United States Department of Agriculture]], [[European Space Agency]], and the [[American Society of Plant Biologists]] (ASPB). She has served as a manuscript reviewer and on the editorial boards for over 15 scientific journals such as the [[American Journal of Botany]], [[The Plant Cell|Plant Cell]], and [[Plant Physiology (journal)|Plant Physiology]]. Wyatt is currently the Education Committee Chair for ASPB and holds this position through 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://aspb.org/about/committees/#toggle-id-5|title=ASPB {{!}} Committees|website=aspb.org|language=en-US|access-date=2017-07-18}}</ref>
